stageDescription: What each framework addresses and when to reach for it.
title: EU AI Act

stops.title: In one line
stops.contentMd:
## In one line

The EU AI Act is a risk-based EU law that sorts AI by how much harm its use could cause people (banned, high-risk, transparency-risk, minimal) and sets heavier rules the higher the risk.

## Explained like you're 10

Think of a school playground with four kinds of games:

- **Banned games.** Pushing people off the climbing frame. Not allowed, ever, whatever the excuse.
- **Supervised games.** The trampoline. You can use it, but only after it's checked for safety, with a teacher watching, and with a record of who used it.
- **Games with a sign.** The splash pool has a sign saying "floor may be wet". You can play, but you must be told.
- **Free play.** Hopscotch. Nobody needs a rule for it.

The EU AI Act does the same for AI. A system that tricks people into harming themselves is banned. A system that decides who gets a loan or a job is the trampoline: allowed, but checked, supervised and recorded. A chatbot is the splash pool: it must tell you it's a robot. A spam filter is hopscotch.

The key idea: **the rules depend on what the AI is used for, not how clever it is.** The same face-recognition software is hopscotch when it unlocks your phone and nearly banned when police scan a crowd with it.

## Why it exists

The EU wanted two things at once: protect people's safety and fundamental rights from AI harms, and give businesses one clear rulebook instead of 27 national ones.

It borrowed an idea Europe already used for toys, lifts and medical devices: **prove a product is safe before it reaches the market**, document how, and put a CE mark on it. High-risk AI is treated the same way. That's why the Act reads like product-safety law: it is one.

| When | What happened |
| --- | --- |
| Apr 2021 | Commission proposes the Act. ChatGPT doesn't exist yet. |
| Nov 2022 | ChatGPT launches. One model now serves thousands of uses, which breaks the "risk by use" logic. |
| Dec 2023 | Political deal, adding rules for general-purpose AI models. |
| Jul 2024 | Published as Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. |
| Aug 2024 | Enters into force. Rules switch on in stages. |
| 2026 | Digital Omnibus delays high-risk rules because standards and guidance aren't ready. |

It is a **regulation**, not a directive: it applies directly in every EU country without national laws copying it.

## Level 1: What counts, who, where

### What counts as an "AI system" (Article 3)

A machine-based system that works with some autonomy and **infers** from its inputs how to produce outputs (predictions, content, recommendations, decisions) that can affect the physical or digital world.

The test word is *infers*. A calculator follows fixed rules you wrote, so it isn't AI. A model that learned from data what a risky loan looks like is.

### Who it applies to

| Role | Plain meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Provider | Builds the AI or sells it under their name | A fintech that builds a credit-scoring model |
| Deployer | Uses the AI in their professional work | A bank that buys that model and uses it on applicants |
| Importer, distributor | Brings it into the EU or passes it on | A reseller |
| Affected person | The human the AI is used on | The loan applicant |

Providers carry most of the duties, because they built it. Deployers carry duties about how they use it.

### Where it applies (Article 2)

It reaches outside Europe. It applies to a provider anywhere in the world that sells AI into the EU, and to a provider or deployer anywhere whose AI **output is used in the EU**. A US company scoring EU customers is in scope. A UK bank scoring UK customers is not.

**Not covered:** military and national security use, AI used only for scientific research, purely personal non-professional use, and (partly) free open-source models.

## The risk pyramid

Most AI sits at the wide bottom with no new duties. General-purpose AI models sit outside the pyramid on their own track (Level 4).

## Level 2: Banned practices (Article 5)

Bans have applied since 2 Feb 2025. Fines go up to 35m euro or 7% of global turnover.

**Why ban instead of control?** With a high-risk system, harm comes from the AI *failing* (bias, errors), and controls can fix that. With a banned practice, harm comes from the AI *working exactly as designed*. No control can fix a purpose that is itself the harm.

| Article | Banned | Like you're 10 | Why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 5(1)(a) | Subliminal, manipulative or deceptive techniques that materially distort behaviour and cause significant harm | An app that secretly flashes messages to make you spend all your pocket money | Takes away your free choice |
| 5(1)(b) | Exploiting vulnerability from age, disability or social or economic situation | A game that targets lonely kids to keep them buying | Targets those least able to resist |
| 5(1)(c) | Social scoring leading to unjustified or disproportionate bad treatment | Getting no school trip because your parents paid a bill late | Punishes people for unrelated things |
| 5(1)(d) | Predicting an individual will commit a crime based only on profiling or personality | Being sent to detention because a computer thinks kids "like you" misbehave | Punishes who you are, not what you did |
| 5(1)(e) | Untargeted scraping of face images from the internet or CCTV to build recognition databases | Someone collecting every class photo online to track everyone | Mass surveillance without consent |
| 5(1)(f) | Emotion recognition in workplaces and education (medical and safety use excepted) | A camera that tells the teacher you look bored | Power imbalance, and the science is weak |
| 5(1)(g) | Biometric categorisation inferring race, political views, union membership, religion, sex life or orientation | A camera guessing your religion from your face | Enables discrimination on sensitive traits |
| 5(1)(h) | Real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces by police | Cameras recognising everyone walking down the street, live | Chills public life |
| New (Dec 2026) | AI generating non-consensual intimate imagery or child sexual abuse material ("nudifier" apps) | Apps that fake naked pictures of real people | Added by the 2026 Omnibus |

**The one ban with exceptions: 5(1)(h).** Police may use live face recognition to search for abduction or trafficking victims, prevent an imminent threat to life or a terror attack, or locate suspects of serious crimes, and only with prior judicial or independent authorisation.

**Advanced point.** Each ban has precise conditions, so classification is a legal test, not a label. Emotion recognition on *customers* is not banned (only workplaces and education are), but it is high-risk. The Commission published interpretive guidelines on Article 5 in Feb 2025.

## Level 3: High-risk AI

This is the core of the Act and most of a consultant's work. High-risk AI is allowed, but only after it's proven safe, and it must stay supervised.

### Step 1: Is it high-risk? (Article 6)

There are two doors in.

**Door 1, Annex I (products).** The AI is a product, or a safety part of one, already covered by EU product law (toys, medical devices, machinery, lifts, cars) and that product needs a third-party safety check. Example: AI that controls a surgical robot.

**Door 2, Annex III (eight areas of life).**

| # | Area | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Biometrics | Remote face identification, emotion recognition |
| 2 | Critical infrastructure | AI managing the electricity grid or water supply |
| 3 | Education | AI marking exams or deciding admissions |
| 4 | Employment | CV screening, promotion or firing decisions, monitoring staff performance |
| 5 | Essential services | Credit scoring, life and health insurance pricing, public benefits, emergency call triage. Fraud detection is excluded. |
| 6 | Law enforcement | Assessing evidence reliability, victim risk |
| 7 | Migration and borders | Assessing visa or asylum applications |
| 8 | Justice and democracy | Helping judges, influencing elections |

**The escape hatch, Article 6(3).** An Annex III system is *not* high-risk if it poses no significant risk because it only does a narrow procedural task, improves a finished human task, spots patterns without replacing human judgement, or does preparatory work. **But any Annex III system that profiles people is always high-risk.** A provider using this escape hatch must document why and still register the system.

Like you're 10: a spell-checker on an exam essay touches education, but it only tidies work you already wrote, so it isn't the trampoline.

### Step 2: What the provider must do (Articles 9-17)

Think of a car maker before a car goes on sale.

| Article | Requirement | Car-maker version |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 9 | Risk management system, for the whole lifecycle | Keep finding and fixing dangers, not just once |
| 10 | Data governance: quality, representativeness, bias checks | Use good parts from known suppliers |
| 11 + Annex IV | Technical documentation | The full engineering manual |
| 12 | Automatic logging | A black box recorder |
| 13 | Instructions for use for the deployer | The owner's manual |
| 14 | Human oversight: a person can understand, override, stop it | Brakes and a steering wheel |
| 15 | Accuracy, robustness, cybersecurity | Crash tests and locks |
| 17 | Quality management system | The factory's quality process |

Then: **conformity assessment** (Article 43; mostly a self-check under Annex VI, a notified body for some biometrics), **EU declaration of conformity** (47), **CE mark** (48), **registration** in the EU database (49), **post-market monitoring** (72) and **serious incident reporting** (73).

### Step 3: What the deployer must do (Articles 26-27)

The person driving the car.

- Use it as the instructions say.
- Assign trained people to oversee it.
- Make sure input data is relevant.
- Monitor it and report risks and serious incidents.
- Keep logs for at least six months.
- Tell workers before using it on them, and tell people when it's used to make decisions about them.
- **Fundamental rights impact assessment (Article 27)** before use, if you are a public body, a private body providing public services, or using it for **credit scoring or life and health insurance pricing**.

### Advanced points

- **You can become the provider by accident (Article 25).** A deployer that substantially modifies a high-risk system, changes its intended purpose, or puts its own name on it takes on the provider's duties.
- **Right to explanation (Article 86).** A person affected by a high-risk AI decision with significant effects can ask the deployer for a clear explanation of the AI's role.
- **Bias data (Article 10(5)).** Providers may process sensitive personal data strictly to detect and correct bias. The 2026 Omnibus extends this beyond high-risk systems.
stops.artifactPrompt: Pick 3 AI systems you've used, built, or can clearly describe. For each: is it an AI system under Article 3 (does it *infer*)? Which tier — banned, high-risk, transparency, or minimal? Which specific article puts it there? Write it up as a short table.

stops.title: Level 4: Transparency and general-purpose AI
stops.contentMd:
## Level 4: Transparency and general-purpose AI

### Transparency obligations (Article 50, applies from 2 Aug 2026)

The splash-pool sign: you can use it, but people must be told. These duties can apply on top of high-risk duties.

| Duty | Who | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tell people they're talking to AI, unless obvious | Provider | A bank's customer chatbot says "I'm an AI assistant" |
| Mark AI-generated audio, images, video and text in a machine-readable way | Provider of generative AI | Invisible watermark in generated images |
| Inform people exposed to emotion recognition or biometric categorisation | Deployer | Call centre tells customers voice analytics is in use |
| Disclose deepfakes, and AI-generated text published to inform the public | Deployer | A label on a synthetic video |

The 2026 Omnibus gave generative systems already on the market before 2 Aug 2026 until 2 Dec 2026 to add watermarking. New systems get no grace period.

### General-purpose AI models (Articles 51-56, applied from 2 Aug 2025)

**Why this was added late:** the original 2021 draft regulated AI by use. Then ChatGPT showed one model can serve thousands of uses. So lawmakers added rules at the **model** level, upstream of every use.

Like you're 10: if a factory sells flour to a thousand bakeries, you check the flour at the factory, not only each cake.

**All GPAI providers (Article 53):** technical documentation; information for downstream providers building on the model; a copyright compliance policy; a public summary of training content. Free open-source models are partly exempt.

**GPAI with systemic risk (Articles 51, 55):** presumed when training compute exceeds 10^25 FLOPs, or designated by the Commission. Extra duties: model evaluations including adversarial testing, assessing and mitigating systemic risks, serious incident reporting, cybersecurity.

**Code of Practice (July 2025):** the voluntary route for providers to show compliance. Fines for GPAI providers: up to 15m euro or 3%, enforceable from Aug 2026.

**Advanced point.** A bank building a chatbot on a third-party model is not the GPAI provider. It is the provider (or deployer) of the *AI system* built on top, and relies on the model provider's Article 53 information.

## Level 5: Enforcement, timeline and how it connects

### Who enforces it

| Body | Role |
| --- | --- |
| AI Office (inside the European Commission) | Supervises general-purpose AI models; after the Omnibus, also AI systems built by the same provider on its own GPAI model |
| AI Board | Member-state representatives; keeps application consistent across the EU |
| National market surveillance authorities | Enforce on the ground: inspections, fines, withdrawing systems. Financial-sector AI stays with financial supervisors |
| Notified bodies | Independent checkers for conformity assessments that need a third party |
| Scientific panel and advisory forum | Technical experts and stakeholders advising the AI Office |

### Penalties (Article 99)

| Breach | Maximum fine |
| --- | --- |
| Banned practices | 35m euro or 7% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher |
| Most other obligations (high-risk, transparency) | 15m euro or 3% |
| Incorrect or misleading information to authorities | 7.5m euro or 1% |

For SMEs and start-ups, the *lower* of the two amounts applies.

### Timeline

Annex III (credit scoring, hiring, insurance pricing) is the date most clients plan around.

**The 2026 Digital Omnibus** delayed the high-risk dates because harmonised standards (written by CEN-CENELEC JTC 21) and Commission guidance weren't ready. It also softened AI literacy (Article 4) to "support the development of" literacy, added the nudifier ban, extended bias-detection data processing to all AI systems, and pushed national sandboxes to Aug 2027. Bans, GPAI duties and Article 50 did not move.

### How it connects to other rules

- **GDPR still applies in full.** The AI Act regulates the AI system; GDPR regulates the personal data inside it. A fundamental rights impact assessment can build on an existing DPIA.
- **Harmonised standards.** Once published, following them gives a "presumption of conformity": the easiest way to prove compliance.
- **ISO/IEC 42001** supports the quality management system (Article 17) but does not equal AI Act compliance. The Act has product-level duties 42001 doesn't cover.
- **Sandboxes (Article 57) and real-world testing (Article 60)** let firms test AI under regulator supervision before full compliance.
- **Sector law stays.** Banks still answer to financial regulators. The Omnibus lets the Commission limit AI Act duties that duplicate sector rules.
stops.artifactPrompt: Pick a GenAI feature you know of (real or plausible). Work out: who is its GPAI provider, does it have systemic risk (10^25 FLOPs test), and what Article 50 transparency duties apply to whoever deploys it? Write the reasoning, not just the conclusion.

stops.title: Worked example: LoanLeaf, a fictional EU lender
stops.contentMd:
## Worked example: LoanLeaf, a fictional EU lender

LoanLeaf, a lender in Ireland, wants two AI tools: a credit-scoring model bought from a vendor, ScoreCo, and a customer chatbot built in-house on a third-party large language model.

### Tool 1: the credit-scoring model

1. **Is it an AI system?** Yes. It learned from past loans to infer default risk.
2. **Banned?** No. It doesn't manipulate, social-score, or use sensitive biometric traits.
3. **High-risk?** Yes. Creditworthiness evaluation is Annex III point 5(b). The 6(3) escape hatch fails because it profiles individuals.
4. **Roles.** ScoreCo is the provider. LoanLeaf is the deployer.
5. **ScoreCo must:** run a risk management system, prove data quality and bias checks, write technical documentation, build in logging and human-override features, pass a conformity assessment, CE-mark it, register it, and give LoanLeaf instructions for use.
6. **LoanLeaf must:** complete a fundamental rights impact assessment before first use (credit scoring triggers Article 27), follow the instructions, assign trained underwriters to oversee decisions, keep logs at least six months, monitor and report serious incidents, tell applicants AI is used, and explain decisions on request (Article 86).
7. **The trap.** LoanLeaf's data team wants to retrain ScoreCo's model on LoanLeaf's own data. That may be a substantial modification, which would make LoanLeaf the provider (Article 25), with all of ScoreCo's duties. This needs a decision before anyone touches the model.
8. **When.** From 2 Dec 2027. Starting now still leaves only about a year to build the evidence.

### Tool 2: the customer chatbot

1. **High-risk?** No, as long as it only answers questions and doesn't decide credit.
2. **Transparency.** Yes. It must tell customers they're talking to AI (Article 50, already applies).
3. **GPAI.** LoanLeaf is not the GPAI provider. It relies on the model provider's documentation.
4. **Scope creep.** If the chatbot later pre-approves loans, it becomes high-risk. The AI inventory must flag purpose changes.

### What a consultant would deliver

An inventory with each system's role and tier, a gap analysis against the obligations, an FRIA template, contract clauses for ScoreCo (documentation, logs, change notice), an oversight procedure for underwriters, and a roadmap to Dec 2027.
stops.artifactPrompt: Using the same 8-step method as LoanLeaf's credit-scoring model, classify one AI tool from your own background (or a plausible one in your target industry): AI system? Banned? High-risk and why? Provider vs deployer? What must each party do? Any 'trap' like LoanLeaf's retraining issue?

stops.title: Applied to your CV
stops.contentMd:
## Applied to your CV

How it could have been applied, not what you did. Barclays UK serving UK customers was outside the Act's scope. The exercise below assumes the same systems served EU customers. In an interview, say: "The Act didn't apply, but this is how I'd classify them if it had." That answers "have you worked on the EU AI Act?" far better than "UK doesn't follow it."

| Project | AI system? | Tier | Why | Key duties if in scope |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Help Hub RAG assistant | Yes | Minimal (likely) | Internal tool, agents know it's AI, it informs people but makes no decision about customers | AI literacy training for agents (Art 4). Voluntary: human-oversight design benchmarked on Art 14 |
| Mortgage rate selector (AVM-driven) | Yes (the AVM is a trained model) | Arguable: likely not Annex III 5(b) | It values a property and filters eligible deals; it doesn't assess the person's creditworthiness. A cautious firm treats it as near-high-risk | If treated as high-risk: deployer duties, FRIA, explanation on request (Art 86). Your LTV-breakdown fix maps to Art 86, not Art 13 |
| Call AI: dissatisfaction detection | Yes | High-risk if it reads voice tone; minimal if it reads transcript text | Voice is biometric data, so voice-based emotion detection is emotion recognition (Annex III 1(c)) | Full high-risk duties + Art 50(3): tell customers voice analytics is in use |
| Same tool aimed at agents | Yes | **Banned** if it reads voice tone | Emotion recognition in the workplace, Art 5(1)(f) | Redesign or stop |
| Call AI: vulnerability detection (text) | Yes | Minimal or limited | Text-based, no biometric data, supports the agent, no automated decision | Literacy, logging good practice; GDPR governs the health data inferred |
| COI automation | **No** | Out of scope | Deterministic rules; nothing is inferred | None under the Act; normal controls apply |

### What this shows an interviewer

1. You know the **definition** test (COI is not AI).
2. You know classification depends on **use and data type** (voice vs text).
3. You know the **same tool** can be high-risk or banned depending on **who** it's used on.
4. You map fixes to the **right article** (Art 86, not Art 13).

## Free videos and courses

Free only, official sources first. Suggested path: 1, then 2, then 8 (about 2 hours). Add 4 for consultant depth. YouTube links come from official EU pages; Claude could not play them directly. Videos from 2024 and early 2025 predate the 2026 Digital Omnibus, so trust the timeline above for dates.

### Videos

| # | Resource | Source | Length | Level | Why watch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | [Introduction to the AI Act (AI4GOV)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w_EN3JM4OI0) | EU-funded project, listed on the [EU Digital Skills platform](https://digital-skills-jobs.europa.eu/en/learning-space/resources/introduction-ai-act-ai4gov-video-resource) | Short | Beginner | First overview: classification, main elements, rollout |
| 2 | [AI Pact webinar 1: Architecture of the AI Act](https://youtube.com/live/eLlSXs1f9Jc) | European AI Office ([event page](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/events/webinar-exploring-architecture-ai-act)), Nov 2024 | ~90 min | Core | The regulator explains the risk pyramid and governance |
| 3 | [AI Pact webinar 2: Architecture, part 2](https://www.youtube.com/live/TzB1IOXdtFw) | European AI Office ([event page](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/events/second-webinar-architecture-ai-act)), Dec 2024 | ~90 min | Core | Feb 2025 obligations, GPAI models, high-risk requirements and standards |
| 4 | [AI Office webinar: risk management logic and standards](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/events/1st-european-ai-office-webinar-risk-management-logic-ai-act-and-related-standards) | European AI Office, May 2024 | Not stated | Advanced | How Article 9 risk management links to harmonised standards |
| 5 | [EU AI Act: A firsthand perspective](https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/seminars/wednesday/video/20250205-1500-t226495.html) | University of Cambridge seminar, Feb 2025 | 49 min | Core | Academic talk; speaker not named on the page |
| 9 | [The EU simplifies the AI Act and bans nudifier apps](https://www.euronews.com/2026/05/20/the-eu-simplifies-the-ai-act-and-bans-nudifier-apps) | Euronews, May 2026 | Short | Update | The only one covering the Omnibus; contents not confirmed |

### Courses and reading

| # | Resource | Format | Length | Catch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6 | [CeADAR: AI for You, Intro to AI and the EU AI Act](https://ceadar-edih-skills-training.teachable.com/courses/2729039) | Self-paced videos and quizzes, EU and Ireland funded | ~3 hrs | Free, but described as open to Irish enterprises and public sector; enrolment may be refused |
| 7 | [BSI: Understanding the Foundations of the EU AI Act](https://www.coursera.org/learn/understanding-the-foundations-of-the-eu-ai-act) (Coursera) | Self-paced | ~2 hrs | "Enroll for free", but full materials may need the paid certificate. Updated May 2026 |
| 8 | [PwC UK: The EU AI Act Explained](https://www.pwc.co.uk/events/in-house-legal-academy/eu-ai-act-explained.html) | Free webinar transcript, Mar 2025 | ~20 min read | Transcript only; good case study on an employee-performance AI tool |

Left out: [KI-Campus EU AI Act Essentials](https://ki-campus.org/en/learning-opportunities/courses/eu-ai-act-essentials) is free and thorough (8 hrs) but German only.

This becomes a reusable interview answer.

stops.title: Interview questions
stops.contentMd:
## Interview questions

| Question | Crisp answer |
| --- | --- |
| Explain the EU AI Act in 10 seconds | A risk-based EU law that sorts AI by the harm its use can cause, banned, high-risk, transparency, minimal, with heavier rules the higher the tier. |
| Why is it risk-based? | Regulating all AI equally would either crush harmless tools or miss dangerous ones. Proportionality aims the effort where people can be hurt. |
| Why are some practices banned outright? | Their harm comes from the AI working as designed, so no control can fix it. |
| How do you classify a system? | Is it an AI system? Banned under Art 5? High-risk via Annex I or Annex III, after the 6(3) test? Transparency duties under Art 50? Otherwise minimal. Then decide provider or deployer. |
| Provider vs deployer? | Provider builds or brands it and carries the product duties (Arts 9-17, conformity, CE). Deployer uses it: oversight, logs, monitoring, FRIA for credit and insurance. |
| A client wants to keep a prohibited use case. What do you advise? | Confirm the exact Art 5 conditions are met. If they are, there's no compliance route: redesign the purpose, population or data, or keep it out of the EU. Renaming isn't redesign. |
| What changed in 2026? | The Digital Omnibus delayed Annex III to Dec 2027 and Annex I to Aug 2028, added a nudifier ban, softened AI literacy. Bans, GPAI and Art 50 didn't move. |
| Does ISO 42001 make you AI Act compliant? | No. It supports the quality management system in Art 17, but the Act has product-level duties it doesn't cover. |
| Have you worked on it? | "It wasn't in scope for Barclays UK, but I used it as a benchmark, and here's how I'd classify those systems..." (see Applied to your CV). |

quiz.question: Explain the EU AI Act in 10 seconds.
quiz.answer: A risk-based EU law that sorts AI by the harm its use can cause: banned, high-risk, transparency, minimal, with heavier rules the higher the tier.
quiz.explanation: This is the one-sentence version you should be able to say without hesitation in an interview.

quiz.question: Why is the Act risk-based rather than applying one rule to all AI?
quiz.answer: Regulating all AI equally would either crush harmless tools or miss dangerous ones.
quiz.explanation: Proportionality aims the compliance effort where people can actually be hurt.

quiz.question: Why are some practices banned outright instead of just controlled?
quiz.answer: Their harm comes from the AI working exactly as designed.
quiz.explanation: No control can fix a purpose that is itself the harm — that's the line between 'banned' and 'high-risk but allowed'.

quiz.question: What's the step-by-step way to classify an AI system under the Act?
quiz.answer: Is it an AI system? Banned under Art 5? High-risk via Annex I or Annex III (after the 6(3) escape-hatch test)? Transparency duties under Art 50? Otherwise minimal. Then decide provider or deployer.
quiz.explanation: This sequence is the actual legal test, not a vibe — walk through it in that order.

quiz.question: What's the difference between a provider and a deployer, and what does each owe?
quiz.answer: Provider builds or brands it and carries the product duties (Arts 9-17, conformity, CE). Deployer uses it: oversight, logs, monitoring, FRIA for credit and insurance.
quiz.explanation: You can become a provider 'by accident' under Article 25 if you substantially modify a high-risk system.

quiz.question: A client wants to keep a prohibited (banned) use case. What do you advise?
quiz.answer: Confirm the exact Article 5 conditions are actually met. If they are, there's no compliance route — redesign the purpose, population or data, or keep it out of the EU. Renaming isn't redesign.
quiz.explanation: Banned practices have no compliance path, unlike high-risk ones.

quiz.question: What changed with the 2026 Digital Omnibus?
quiz.answer: It delayed Annex III high-risk obligations to Dec 2027 and Annex I to Aug 2028, added a ban on 'nudifier' apps, and softened the AI literacy requirement. Bans, GPAI duties and Article 50 transparency did not move.
quiz.explanation: Know which parts moved and which didn't — this is a common 'what's current' interview check.

quiz.question: Does being ISO/IEC 42001 certified make you EU AI Act compliant?
quiz.answer: No. It supports the quality management system required by Article 17, but the Act has product-level duties (conformity assessment, CE marking, registration) that 42001 doesn't cover.
quiz.explanation: A very common trap question — frameworks are not interchangeable with legal compliance.

stops.artifactPrompt: Record yourself answering 3 of these questions out loud, unscripted, in under 30 seconds each. Write down which ones you fumbled and why.

stops.title: Self-check
stops.contentMd:
## Self-check

Answer out loud before reading the answers.

1. A US company scores EU job applicants with AI from its US office. In scope?
2. A call centre detects customer frustration from voice tone. Banned, high-risk or minimal?
3. The same tool monitors the call-centre staff. Now?
4. Name three things a deployer of a high-risk system must do.
5. A bank fine-tunes a vendor's credit model on its own data. What's the risk?
6. What does training compute above 10^25 FLOPs trigger?
7. Maximum fine for a banned practice?

**Answers:** (1) Yes, the output is used in the EU. (2) High-risk: emotion recognition from biometric data, Annex III 1(c), plus Art 50(3) disclosure. (3) Banned, Art 5(1)(f), emotion recognition at work. (4) Any three of: follow instructions, human oversight, relevant input data, monitor and report, keep logs 6 months, inform workers and affected people, FRIA where required. (5) A substantial modification could make the bank the provider (Art 25). (6) Presumption of a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk (Art 51). (7) 35m euro or 7% of global turnover, whichever is higher.

quiz.question: A US company scores EU job applicants with AI from its US office. In scope?
quiz.explanation: The Act applies wherever the AI's output is used in the EU, regardless of where the provider is based.

quiz.question: A call centre detects customer frustration from voice tone. Banned, high-risk, or minimal?
quiz.explanation: Voice is biometric data, so voice-based emotion detection is emotion recognition under Annex III 1(c), plus Article 50(3) disclosure duties.

quiz.question: The same voice-tone tool is now used to monitor call-centre staff instead of customers. What changes?
quiz.answer: It becomes banned, not just high-risk.
quiz.explanation: Emotion recognition in the workplace is banned outright under Article 5(1)(f) — same technology, different population, different tier.

quiz.question: Name three things a deployer of a high-risk system must do.
quiz.answer: Any three of: follow instructions, assign human oversight, ensure relevant input data, monitor and report, keep logs 6 months, inform workers/affected people, complete an FRIA where required.
quiz.explanation: These are the Article 26-27 deployer duties, distinct from the provider's build-time duties.

quiz.question: A bank fine-tunes a vendor's credit-scoring model on its own data. What risk does this create?
quiz.answer: The bank could become the provider by accident (Article 25) if the fine-tuning counts as a substantial modification.
quiz.explanation: This inherits all of the original provider's duties — conformity assessment, documentation, CE marking.

quiz.question: What does training compute above 10^25 FLOPs trigger?
quiz.answer: A presumption that the model is a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk (Article 51).
quiz.explanation: This triggers extra duties: adversarial testing, systemic risk mitigation, incident reporting, cybersecurity.

quiz.question: What's the maximum fine for a banned practice?
quiz.answer: 35 million euro or 7% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher.
quiz.explanation: This is the highest penalty tier in the Act — most other obligations cap at 15m/3%.
